name: Bhaktajaneswarar Temple, Thirunavalur
deity: Shiva as Bhaktajaneswarar (Thirunavaleswarar), with the goddess Manonmani (Sundaranayaki)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu and the birthplace of Sundarar, who sang it in the Tevaram (8th century); rebuilt in stone by the Chola prince Rajaditya in the 10th century
dynasty: Chola (Rajaditya, son of Parantaka I), with later Chola inscriptions
summary: Thirunavalur is the home village of Sundarar, youngest of the three Tevaram saints, and its Bhaktajaneswarar temple was rebuilt in stone by a Chola prince who later fell at the battle of Takkolam.

sections.history: Thirunavalur, on the road from Viluppuram to Kedilam, is honoured above all as the birthplace of Sundarar, born Nambi Aruran in the eighth century, the last of the three saints whose hymns make up the Tevaram. Its temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted among the shrines of Nadu Nadu; Sundarar himself sang the Lord of his native place. The temple's own inscriptions tell its later story. A record of the twenty-eighth year of Parantaka I states that his eldest son, Rajaditya, rebuilt it in stone, replacing an earlier brick shrine, and from the next year it was called Rajadityeswaram. Rajaditya was killed soon after at the battle of Takkolam, an event recalled in records of the Rashtrakuta king Krishna III found here. Inscriptions of Rajaraja I, Kulothunga I and Rajendra III follow.
sections.architecture: The temple is an early Chola stone shrine of the Dravidian style, enlarged over the centuries with enclosures, mandapas and a separate shrine for the goddess Manonmani. In the north-eastern corner of the precinct is a shrine to Sundarar, who stands with his two consorts, Paravai Nachiyar of Tiruvarur and Sangili Nachiyar of Thiruvottriyur, one on either side. A short walk down the street, a newer temple to Sundarar stands on the site held to be his family home.
sections.legends: The shrine's story is Sundarar's own. Born here to a devout family, the boy was brought up by the local chieftain Narasinga Munaiyar, and he grew into the poet whom Shiva claimed as his servant and friend. The Lord's name here, Bhaktajaneswarar, the Lord of his devotees, suits a village that gave the Tevaram one of its greatest singers. Devotees believe that Sundarar received the Lord's grace in this very shrine before his wanderings took him across the Tamil land.
sections.festivals: Sundarar's guru puja, kept in the Tamil month of Aadi on the day of his nakshatra, Swathi, is the great day of the village, when the saint is honoured in his birthplace. Maha Shivaratri, Arudra Darshanam and the monthly Pradosham are also observed. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thirunavalur is a pilgrimage for anyone who loves the Tevaram. Worship at the old Chola sanctum, look for the inscribed walls that name Rajaditya, and pause before Sundarar standing between his two consorts. Then walk down the street to the shrine on the site of his home, where the story of a saint who called Shiva his friend began.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Thirunavalur lies on the Viluppuram–Kedilam road, roughly 25 km south-west of Viluppuram and close to the Chennai–Tiruchirappalli highway near Ulundurpet. Viluppuram Junction is the nearest major railway station; Puducherry is the nearest airport, with Chennai and Tiruchirappalli the nearest international airports.
